subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A male newborn is noted to have abdominal distention and bilious vomiting in the first day of life. He has not passed meconium by 48 hours of age. A digital rectal examination triggers an explosive expulsion of stool, and the rectum is found to be empty on examination. His mother had a sibling with Down syndrome.
question: Which of the following best explains this neonate's failure to pass meconium?

options.text: A meconium plug causing neonatal small bowel obstruction
Absence of ganglion cells in a distal colonic segment
Persistence of the vitelline duct with an ileal outpouching
Hypertrophy of Peyer patches acting as an intestinal lead point
Failure of the midgut to rotate around the superior mesenteric artery

explanation_correct: This neonate has Hirschsprung disease (congenital megacolon), in which a distal segment of colon lacks ganglion cells and enteric nervous plexuses, so it cannot relax and functions as a functional obstruction. This causes failure to pass meconium within 48 hours, abdominal distention, and bilious emesis. The empty rectum and explosive 'squirt sign' on digital examination are classic, and there is an increased risk with Down syndrome.

explanation_incorrect.A: A meconium plug causes meconium ileus (classically with cystic fibrosis), a different neonatal obstruction without an aganglionic segment or the squirt sign.
explanation_incorrect.C: A persistent vitelline duct is Meckel diverticulum, a congenital ileal lesion that can present with bleeding or obstruction but not failure to pass meconium from an aganglionic colon.
explanation_incorrect.D: Hypertrophied Peyer patches can act as a lead point for intussusception after viral illness, which causes intermittent pain and currant jelly stools in infants, not delayed meconium at birth.
explanation_incorrect.E: Failed midgut rotation causes malrotation with Ladd bands and bilious obstruction, but it does not produce the empty rectum and squirt sign of an aganglionic distal colon.

educationalObjective: Hirschsprung disease is an aganglionic distal colon causing failure to pass meconium within 48 hours, distention, bilious emesis, and an empty rectum.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: An infant with presumed Hirschsprung disease undergoes genetic testing that reveals a loss-of-function mutation. The affected bowel segment lacks the normal network of enteric neurons and shows absence of both the submucosal and myenteric plexuses on biopsy. The defect is traced to a failure of neural crest cells to populate the distal gut.
question: Which of the following genes and plexus findings best match this patient's disease?

options.text: Gain-of-function RET mutation with intact Auerbach and Meissner plexuses
APC mutation with hyperplastic Auerbach plexus
KRAS mutation with absent Meissner plexus but intact Auerbach plexus
CFTR mutation with an absent myenteric plexus
Loss-of-function RET mutation with absent Auerbach and Meissner plexuses

explanation_correct: Hirschsprung disease results from failure of neural crest cell migration, associated with loss-of-function mutations in RET ('RET mutation in the REcTum'). The aganglionic distal segment lacks ganglion cells of both the myenteric (Auerbach) and submucosal (Meissner) plexuses, so the bowel cannot relax and proximal stool accumulates.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hirschsprung involves loss of function (not gain of function) of RET, and the plexuses are absent, not intact; intact plexuses would permit normal relaxation.
explanation_incorrect.B: APC mutations drive the chromosomal instability pathway of adenomatous polyps and colorectal cancer, not congenital aganglionosis.
explanation_incorrect.C: KRAS mutations are involved in adenomatous polyp malignant transformation, not Hirschsprung, and both plexuses—not just Meissner—are absent in the aganglionic segment.
explanation_incorrect.D: CFTR mutations cause cystic fibrosis, which can produce meconium ileus, but the enteric plexuses are present; the myenteric plexus is absent in Hirschsprung, not CF.

educationalObjective: Hirschsprung disease is linked to loss-of-function RET mutations and absent Auerbach and Meissner ganglion cells from failed neural crest migration.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 4-month-old infant with chronic constipation undergoes a contrast enema. The rectum is small and collapsed with no retained contrast, while the colon just proximal to it is markedly dilated. A digital rectal examination produces a sudden explosive expulsion of stool. Biopsy of the dilated segment shows normal ganglion cells, whereas the rectal biopsy shows none.
question: Which of the following statements about this infant's imaging and examination findings is correct?

options.text: The dilated proximal colon and collapsed rectum define a transition zone from normally innervated to aganglionic bowel
The dilated segment is aganglionic, while the rectum has intact ganglion cells
The transition zone reflects an area of ischemic injury at the splenic flexure
The empty rectum results from a mechanical tumor obstructing the sigmoid colon
The squirt sign indicates intact ganglion cells throughout the distal colon

explanation_correct: In Hirschsprung disease the aganglionic distal segment (here the rectum) cannot relax and remains collapsed and empty, while the normally innervated proximal colon dilates from the functional obstruction; the junction is the 'transition zone.' The biopsy confirms ganglion cells in the dilated proximal segment and their absence in the rectum. The explosive squirt sign and empty rectum support the diagnosis.

explanation_incorrect.B: The opposite is true: the rectum is aganglionic and collapsed, while the proximal dilated segment has normal ganglion cells, as the biopsy demonstrated.
explanation_incorrect.C: A transition zone between innervated and aganglionic bowel is not an ischemic watershed injury; colonic ischemia occurs at the splenic flexure or rectosigmoid junction with pain and hematochezia.
explanation_incorrect.D: An empty rectum in Hirschsprung reflects the functional obstruction of an aganglionic segment, not a mechanical sigmoid tumor; tumors are lead points for adult intussusception.
explanation_incorrect.E: The squirt sign—explosive expulsion of feces with an empty rectum—supports absent ganglion cells in the distal colon, not intact innervation.

educationalObjective: The transition zone in Hirschsprung disease is the junction between dilated, innervated proximal colon and collapsed, aganglionic distal bowel.

subject: Gastrointestinal
vignette: A 6-month-old child with suspected Hirschsprung disease needs a diagnostic procedure to confirm the absence of ganglion cells in the distal rectum before definitive management. The clinician plans to obtain a rectal specimen that includes submucosa, then proceed to surgical correction if the diagnosis is confirmed.
question: Which of the following pairs the appropriate diagnostic test with the definitive treatment for this child?

options.text: Barium enema only; no surgery required
Technetium-99m pertechnetate scan; chemotherapy
Rectal suction biopsy; surgical resection of the aganglionic segment
Colonoscopic mucosal biopsy; long-term laxative therapy
Ultrasound with target sign; angiographic embolization

explanation_correct: Hirschsprung disease is diagnosed by rectal suction biopsy showing absence of ganglion cells in the submucosal and myenteric plexuses. Definitive treatment is surgical resection of the aganglionic distal segment, so that the normally innervated proximal bowel can be pulled through. This pairs the correct diagnostic test with the correct treatment.

explanation_incorrect.A: A contrast enema can suggest a transition zone but is not definitive; Hirschsprung disease requires biopsy confirmation and surgical resection, not observation alone.
explanation_incorrect.B: A pertechnetate (Meckel) scan detects ectopic gastric mucosa and is not used for Hirschsprung disease; chemotherapy has no role in this congenital aganglionosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Colonoscopic mucosal biopsy may miss the submucosal ganglion cells; the diagnosis uses rectal suction biopsy, and definitive management is resection rather than lifelong laxatives.
explanation_incorrect.E: A target sign on ultrasound suggests intussusception, and angiographic embolization treats bleeding; neither addresses the aganglionic segment of Hirschsprung disease.

educationalObjective: Hirschsprung disease is diagnosed by rectal suction biopsy and definitively treated by resection of the aganglionic segment.
